newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechen presidential campaign turns bitter.
newsitem.headline: Chechen presidential campaign turns bitter.

text.p: Chechnya's presidential campaign took an ugly turn on Monday, with a leading contender launching a bitter attack on his main presidential rivals which threatened the separatist rebels' anti-Russian wartime alliance.

Shamil Basayev, who led a hostage-taking raid in Russia in June 1995 in which more than 100 people were killed, called President Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev and former rebel commander Aslan Maskhadov "crooks".

Basayev, 32, served under the two men during the 21-month conflict against Russian forces which ended last August. But he said he would not work with them if he lost the January 27 election in Chechnya in which all three are running.

"If I do not become president, then I will not stand shoulder to shoulder with those who defeated me, as I cannot stand next to crooks," Basayev told several hundred people outside the Chechen State University in the capital Grozny.
Maskhadov and Yandarbiyev have dismissed Basayev's increasing attacks on them and have denied his accusations.
Basayav said Maskhadov had violated the constitution by becoming prime minister. The post of president and prime minister, he said, should be held by the same person.

"Neither Yandarbiyev nor Maskhadov has done a thing for the people in the six months they have been in power," said Basayev, dressed in a dapper charcoal-coloured greatcoat rather than his usual camouflage fatigues.
Maskhadov's press secretary, Mayerbek Vachagayev, denied Basayev's accusations. "He only has a few more days to spit filth at Maskhadov," he told Reuters.
Maskhadov was chief field commander in the rebels' 21-month war with Russian troops. He is widely viewed as the strongest of 16 candidates and recently resigned as interim prime minister.
The Kremlin withdrew the last of its troops from the tiny mountainous region this month after failing to crush its independence bid in a conflict which killed tens of thousands of people.
Maskhadov, a former colonel in the Soviet army's artillery forces, is keeping a low profile. But he denied he was staying away from the campaign trail because of alleged death threats.

"The war taught me never to take account of threats. There were many situations during the war where I should have been killed, 100 percent," he told reporters at a residence in Pervomaiskaya, five km (three miles) outside Grozny.

"I haven't campaigned much. It just that people have studied me well. Everything I have said is on record. I don't need to improve my rating. The main thing is to have free and fair elections," said the grey-haired commander, speaking surrounded by bodyguards in the backyard of a traditional brick Chechen farmhouse.
The election is a first step in restoring order in Chechnya following last August's peace accord.

Some Russian officials have welcomed the election. Others have hinted that Moscow may not recognise it because voting centres are not being organised for refugees in Russian cities, while Grozny says few refugees are left outside Chechnya.
All the main candidates say Russia is looking for a reason to declare the vote illegitimate.

Chechen officials make no secret that they regard the region as independent, but Russia says it cannot secede. A peace accord signed on August 31 deferred solving the question of Chechnya's status for five years.
